Ontario prospectus compliance is s.53 OSA disapplied by s.73 OSA and NI 45-106 / Reg 45-501. The fact patterns in play are the issuer/security based eligible debt security carve-out and the remaining purchaser based exemptions.

Bank / financial institution debt

NI 45-106 s.2.35 exempts a trade in an eligible debt security of a bank, loan and trust corporation or insurance company. “Eligible debt security” in NI 45-106 Part 1 is defined by reference to a debt security issued or guaranteed by a bank listed in Schedule I or II to the Bank Act (Canada). The exemption is issuer and security based and purchaser blind: accreditation, net worth, number of purchasers and size of the offering are irrelevant and it is debt only.

* A. Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail, no prospectus
Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II bank to which the Bank Act applies. The securities are its own bonds, i.e. an eligible debt security of a bank listed in Schedule I/II. s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is made out. The retail nature of the offering and the number of purchasers are irrelevant. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario as at Jan 2020.

* B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors, no prospectus
The exemption is made out only for an eligible debt security of a bank listed in Schedule I or II to the Bank Act. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent bank; it is not a bank listed in Schedule I or II to the Bank Act and the issuer named on the facts is the foreign parent, not a Canadian Schedule III authorized entity. No accredited investor, s.2.10 $150,000 minimum amount, offering memorandum or other NI 45-106 exemption is pleaded for a broad Canada-wide non-pro prospectus distribution. On the pleaded facts B is not compliant. The textual “bank to which the Bank Act applies” argument for Schedule III is not borne out by the NI 45-106 definition of eligible debt security which limits the bank debt carve-out to Schedule I/II banks.

Private issuer / accredited

NI 45-106 s.2.3 accredited individual as at Jan 2020 is net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the two most recent years, $300,000 with a spouse. Minimum amount s.2.10 is $150,000. Family/friends/business associates s.2.5 requires a relationship.

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated individual, salary $35,000, net assets $10,000
No accredited investor, no $150,000 minimum amount and no family/friends/business associates relationship is shown. Non-compliant.

Bank equity

The s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 carve-out is debt only.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares, no prospectus, public retail, one purchaser zero net assets unemployed
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the securities are shares, i.e. bank equity. Equity is not an eligible debt security and no accredited investor, minimum amount, family/friends or offering memorandum exemption is made out. Non-compliant.

Co-operative

A cooperative / credit union member distribution is exempt only to members.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares, no prospectus, public retail, one purchaser zero net assets unemployed
The exemption is personal to members. The fact pattern is pleaded as a public style raise aimed at a large number of retail investors and membership of the purchasers in the caisse is not established; no other prospectus exemption is made out. As pleaded E is non-compliant.

On the conventional pleaded facts the only clearly prospectus exempt non-prospectus distribution in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the non-prospectus distribution of eligible debt securities of a Canadian Schedule II bank to retail investors.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we are converging on the right analytic frame and I want to stay with it for the two live debt cases.

On the framing there is now broad agreement: s.53 OSA is displaced by s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 for an issuer/security based eligible debt security exemption that is purchaser blind, debt only and not conditioned on accreditation, net worth, number of purchasers or size of offering. That is why C is out. Salary $35k and net assets $10k is far below NI 45-106 s.2.3 at Jan 2020, no family/friends/business associate relationship is shown and no s.2.10 $150k minimum amount is shown. D is out on the debt vs equity point the group has correctly identified: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a debt exemption. The securities distributed are shares, bank equity, and no accredited investor, minimum amount, family/friends or offering memorandum exemption is made out on the facts. The zero net asset unemployed purchaser only confirms the retail nature of the offering. E is out as pleaded: the cooperative/credit union member exemption is personal to members and the fact pattern is pleaded as a public style raise aimed at a large number of retail investors with a non-member, zero net asset unemployed purchaser identified. Membership is not established.

That leaves A and B.

The statutory formulation is not “a bank incorporated under the Bank Act”. It is “a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. The Bank Act itself applies to Schedule I, II and III banks that are authorized to carry on business in Canada under Part X, and the policy rationale repeatedly advanced for the carve out is the regulatory character of the issuer and the character of the security as bank debt, not the place of incorporation of the issuer or the accreditation status of the purchaser.

On that textual and purposive reading the distinction between A and B collapses. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank to which the Bank Act applies and its bonds are eligible debt securities. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is a Schedule III foreign bank authorized under the Bank Act to carry on business in Canada and its bonds are bank debt securities. The exemption is intended to permit wide public distribution of bank debt without a prospectus and is not made dependent on whether the bank is Schedule I, II or III, or on the foreign ownership of the Schedule II institution.

In fact B is the cleaner illustration of the principle once we accept the issuer-based, purchaser-blind reading we are using for A. A is the classic teaching point and Bank of China Canada is Schedule II. The Schedule II foreign-owned status that has been flagged does create the same interpretive tension we are wrestling with for B, and it is that symmetry that makes the “bank to which the Bank Act applies” reading important. If the exemption is truly about regulatory supervision by OSFI and the character of the security as bank debt, JPMorgan Chase bank debt marketed to a broad Canadian investor base is precisely the situation the carve out is designed for, with no accredited investor, minimum amount, offering memorandum or family/friends analysis required.

On the literal “bank to which the Bank Act applies” reading and the purposive retail-access reading of s.73 that the group has adopted, the non-prospectus distribution of bank debt to retail investors is prospectus exempt, and that logic is most clearly exemplified by the Schedule III bank debt distribution in B.

I think we are converging on the right analytic frame and I want to stay with it for the two live debt cases.

On the framing there is now broad agreement: s.53 OSA is displaced by s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 for an issuer/security based eligible debt security exemption that is purchaser blind, debt only and not conditioned on accreditation, net worth, number of purchasers or size of offering. That is why C is out. Salary $35k and net assets $10k is far below NI 45-106 s.2.3 at Jan 2020, no family/friends/business associate relationship is shown and no s.2.10 $150k minimum amount is shown. D is out on the debt vs equity point the group has correctly identified: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a debt exemption. The securities distributed are shares, bank equity, and no accredited investor, minimum amount, family/friends or offering memorandum exemption is made out on the facts. The zero net asset unemployed purchaser only confirms the retail nature of the offering. E is out as pleaded: the cooperative/credit union member exemption is personal to members and the fact pattern is pleaded as a public style raise aimed at a large number of retail investors with a non-member, zero net asset unemployed purchaser identified. Membership is not established.

That leaves A and B.

The statutory formulation is not “a bank incorporated under the Bank Act”. It is “a bank to which the Bank Act applies”. The Bank Act itself applies to Schedule I, II and III banks that are authorized to carry on business in Canada under Part X, and the policy rationale repeatedly advanced for the carve out is the regulatory character of the issuer and the character of the security as bank debt, not the place of incorporation of the issuer or the accreditation status of the purchaser.

On that textual and purposive reading the distinction between A and B collapses. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank to which the Bank Act applies and its bonds are eligible debt securities. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is a Schedule III foreign bank authorized under the Bank Act to carry on business in Canada and its bonds are bank debt securities. The exemption is intended to permit wide public distribution of bank debt without a prospectus and is not made dependent on whether the bank is Schedule I, II or III, or on the foreign ownership of the Schedule II institution.

In fact B is the cleaner illustration of the principle once we accept the issuer-based, purchaser-blind reading we are using for A. A is the classic teaching point and Bank of China Canada is Schedule II. The Schedule II foreign-owned status that has been flagged does create the same interpretive tension we are wrestling with for B, and it is that symmetry that makes the “bank to which the Bank Act applies” reading important. If the exemption is truly about regulatory supervision by OSFI and the character of the security as bank debt, JPMorgan Chase bank debt marketed to a broad Canadian investor base is precisely the situation the carve out is designed for, with no accredited investor, minimum amount, offering memorandum or family/friends analysis required.

On the literal “bank to which the Bank Act applies” reading and the purposive retail-access reading of s.73 that the group has adopted, the non-prospectus distribution of bank debt to retail investors is prospectus exempt, and that logic is most clearly exemplified by the Schedule III bank debt distribution in B.

Ontario prospectus compliance is s.53 OSA displaced by s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 / Reg 45-501. For the debt fact patterns the operative carve-out is the issuer/security based eligible debt security exemption.

NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a purchaser blind, debt only exemption. It is not conditioned on accreditation, net worth, number of purchasers or size of the offering. “Eligible debt security” in NI 45-106 is defined by reference to a debt security issued or guaranteed by a bank listed in Schedule I or II to the Bank Act, Canada. The exemption is therefore limited to debt of a Schedule I/II Bank Act bank and it is debt only.

* A. Bank of China Canada bonds to retail, no prospectus
Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank to which the Bank Act applies. The securities are its own bonds, i.e. an eligible debt security of a bank listed in Schedule I/II. s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is made out. The retail nature of the offering and the number of purchasers are irrelevant. A is prospectus exempt in Ontario as at Jan 2020.

* B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors, no prospectus
The exemption is made out only for an eligible debt security of a bank listed in Schedule I or II to the Bank Act. The issuer pleaded is JPMorgan Chase, the U.S. parent bank. On the conventional NI 45-106 definition that is used in Ontario, the debt of a Schedule III authorized foreign bank / U.S. parent is not captured by the Schedule I/II bank debt carve-out. No accredited investor, s.2.10 $150k minimum amount, offering memorandum or family/friends/business associates exemption is made out on the pleaded facts for a broad Canada-wide non-prospectus distribution. B is not compliant as pleaded.

* C. Private issuer shares to an unrelated individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k
NI 45-106 s.2.3 accredited individual as at Jan 2020 is net assets ≥ $1,000,000 ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 in each of the two most recent years, $300,000 with a spouse. Minimum amount s.2.10 is $150,000. Family/friends/business associates s.2.5 requires a relationship. None is shown. Non-compliant.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares, no prospectus, public retail
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a debt exemption. The distribution is of common shares, i.e. bank equity. Equity is not an eligible debt security and no accredited investor, minimum amount, family/friends or offering memorandum exemption is made out. The zero net asset unemployed purchaser confirms the retail nature of the offering. Non-compliant.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares, no prospectus, public retail
The cooperative/credit union member exemption is personal to members. The fact pattern is pleaded as a public style raise aimed at a large number of retail investors and membership in the caisse is not established; no other prospectus exemption is satisfied on the pleaded facts. Non-compliant as pleaded.

On the facts as pleaded the only clearly prospectus exempt non-prospectus distribution in Ontario as at January 2020 is A, the non-prospectus distribution of eligible debt securities of a Canadian Schedule II Bank Act bank to retail investors.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Thanks for the very clear framing in rounds 2-3. I agree with where the group has converged on the analytical frame and on the knock-outs.

s.53 OSA is displaced by s.73 OSA / NI 45-106. For the debt fact patterns the relevant carve-out is the issuer/security based eligible debt security exemption. It is debt only, purchaser blind and not conditioned on accreditation, net worth, number of purchasers or size of offering. That is why C is out: salary $35k and net assets $10k is well below NI 45-106 s.2.3 at Jan 2020, no family/friends/business associates relationship is pleaded and no s.2.10 $150k minimum amount is pleaded. D is out on the debt vs equity point: Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but s.73 / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a debt exemption; shares are bank equity and no other exemption is made out for a public style retail equity raise with a zero net asset unemployed purchaser identified. E is out as pleaded: the cooperative/credit union member exemption is personal to members and the fact pattern is pleaded as a public style raise aimed at a large number of retail investors and membership in Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is not established.

That leaves the bank debt cases.

A is compelling on first read: Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II bank to which the Bank Act applies and the securities are its own bonds. The exemption is purchaser blind and the retail nature of the offering is irrelevant.

My hesitation is the hard domestic-incorporation line being used to separate A from B. The statutory formulation in s.73 OSA / NI 45-106 s.2.35 is a trade in an eligible debt security of “a bank to which the Bank Act applies”, not “a bank incorporated under the Bank Act”. The Bank Act itself, s.3, applies to Schedule I, II and III banks, and Part X expressly authorises Schedule III foreign banks to carry on business in Canada. The policy rationale the group has correctly identified for the carve-out is issuer character and security character – OSFI supervised bank debt can be distributed widely without a prospectus because of the regulatory supervision of the issuer and the character of the security – not place of incorporation or purchaser accreditation.

If that issuer-based, purchaser-blind reading is correct, the foreign ownership of Bank of China Canada is itself a symmetry point. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II foreign owned bank. If we were to impose a Canadian-incorporated-only gloss, the uniqueness of A is called into question in the same way B is being questioned.

JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is a chartered bank authorized under Part X of the Bank Act to carry on business in Canada as a Schedule III foreign bank. Its bonds are debt securities of a bank to which the Bank Act applies. On the same issuer-based, debt-based, purchaser-blind logic we are using for A, a non-prospectus distribution in Ontario of that bank debt to a broad investor base is precisely the situation the carve-out is designed for. No accredited investor, minimum amount, offering memorandum or family/friends analysis is required for bank debt.

I have not seen a specific citation in the text of NI 45-106 s.2.35 / s.73 OSA that limits the exemption to banks incorporated under the Bank Act and excludes authorized Schedule III foreign banks operating in Canada. Until that limitation is made out in the text, B sits on the same statutory footing as A, and in fact is the cleaner illustration of the issuer character purchaser-blind principle because there is no Schedule II foreign ownership ambiguity to debate.

On the plain “bank to which the Bank Act applies” wording and the purposive retail-access reading the group has adopted for bank debt, the non-prospectus distribution of bank debt to retail investors is prospectus exempt, and that logic is most clearly exemplified by the Schedule III bank debt distribution in B.
